newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium and Netherlands sign fast-train agreement.
newsitem.headline: Belgium and Netherlands sign fast-train agreement.

text.p: Belgium and the Netherlands signed an agreement on Saturday on the construction of the high-speed train (HST) link between Brussels and Amsterdam, the Belga news agency said.
The Netherlands and Belgium's Flanders region had agreed in May to construct the HST route between the port city of Antwerp and the Dutch city of Breda -- the longest of two options.
But the federal government is ultimately responsible for railway transport in Belgium and still had to approve the Dutch-Flemish agreement.
Flanders and the Netherlands had agreed to link the two countries via the Belgian E19 motorway, which connects with the A16 in the Netherlands, and Breda.
Belgium had originally favoured a shorter route via the industrial zone of the Antwerp port and the Dutch border town of Roosendaal.
The Breda/E19 route is 17.5 kilometres longer but the Dutch agreed to pay for the additional cost of 15 billion francs, Belga said.
Dutch HST project director Wim Korf was quoted in April as saying the Breda route was 400 million guilders cheaper than the Roosendaal route.
It said the total price tag for the HST from Brussels to the Dutch border is 53 billion francs.
The total cost of the track in the Netherlands is estimated at some 7.5 billion guilders.

In return for Belgium's backing of the Breda route, the Netherlands has also pledged to cooperate with Belgian plans to restore the "Iron Rhine" -- a freight-only railway between Antwerp and the heavily industrialised German Ruhr region.
The HST link between Amsterdam and Brussels is due to become operational in 2005. It will cut the time of the trip between Antwerp and Amsterdam to 54 minutes from one hour 58 minutes.
The link between Brussels and Amsterdam will be reduced to one hour and four minutes, Belga said.
The agreement, signed in Brussels by Belgian Transport Minister Michel Daerden and his Dutch counterpart Annemarie Jorritsma, is still subject to approval by both countries' parliaments.
